notes:
These notes cover Genesis 39 verse by verse. I was able to read the full Enduring Word (Guzik) and Bible.org (Utley) pages. Wesley, Constable, Clarke, Coffman, Barnes, Gill, Pulpit, Biblical Illustrator, Carson (TGC) and MacArthur (GTY) come only from search-result excerpts. I couldn't load Gill, Ellicott or Pulpit for every verse. I found nothing on netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, the Catholic and Orthodox sites, or about prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching, so those parts are left out.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Guzik: the Hebrew word for "officer" can mean eunuch, but it came to be used for any high court official, so it was possible that Potiphar was a eunuch, though we can't be sure. He says Joseph, as a slave, had no control over where he ended up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-39/
- Utley: since Potiphar was married, he takes the word as a court title. He reads "captain of the guard" as an important royal military post, and the name Potiphar as meaning roughly "he whom the sun god gives." https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- Wesley (Methodist): Joseph was placed with a public official so he could learn public business. What God intends men for, he will be sure, some way or other, to qualify them for. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-39.html

**v. 2**
- Utley: "the LORD" (YHWH) is rare in the Joseph story. The phrase "the LORD was with Joseph" repeats through the chapter, and God, not Joseph, is the central character! The Hebrew verb for "successful" means getting a task done well, not just material blessing. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- Wesley: It is God's presence with us that makes all we do prosperous. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-39.html
- Biblical Illustrator: notes the order of the words. It doesn't say the Lord was with Joseph because he prospered, but that the Lord was with him and so he prospered. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/genesis-39.html

**v. 3**
- Utley: Potiphar promoted Joseph because of his link to God's blessing, not just his skill, and did so strictly for personal gain and not in any religious sense (Utley's words). https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- Guzik: by trusting God and working hard, Joseph showed Potiphar that God was real. Believers' work should show the same. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-39/

**v. 4**
- Utley: the two words for Joseph's role, "personal servant" and "overseer," suggest a household steward, something like an executive secretary today. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- Constable: Joseph proved faithful in a little and therefore the Lord placed him in charge of much. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-39.html

**v. 5**
- Utley: there is a link between physical blessing and being connected to the covenant people (Gen 12:3; 30:27). https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: God blesses those who bless His own people, according to the promise. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/genesis-39.html
- Guzik: in the same way, a believer's godly presence can bring blessing on their workplace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-39/

**v. 6**
- Utley: the one thing Potiphar kept to himself, his food, may reflect the Egyptian custom of keeping separate from foreigners at meals (cf. 43:32). The phrase "handsome in form and appearance" is also used of Joseph's mother Rachel. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- Wesley: the master had the enjoyment and the servant had the work, an example not to be imitated by any master, unless he could be sure that he had one like Joseph for a servant. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-39.html
- Guzik: by his count Joseph spent about 11 years in Potiphar's house. God often lets good things grow slowly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-39/

**v. 7**
- Bible.org (Conquering Temptation): Potiphar's wife noticed Joseph only after he had been raised up. It was when Joseph was successful that he experienced greater temptations. https://bible.org/seriespage/2-conquering-temptation-genesis-39
- Utley: there is a deliberate contrast with Judah in chapter 38. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- Carson (TGC): her offer probably appealed to Joseph's pride and his loneliness. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-temptation-of-joseph-genesis-39-en/

**vv. 8–9**
- Guzik's reasons for Joseph's refusal: he remembered his duty to Potiphar, he remembered she was another man's wife, he called the sin "great wickedness" instead of excusing it, and he knew it was a sin against God, not just a risk of getting caught. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-39/
- Barnes: Joseph was bound by the law of honor, the law of chastity (this great evil), and the law of piety (sin against God). https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cev/genesis/39-16.html
- Utley: Joseph uses the general name *Elohim* because she would not have known the covenant name YHWH. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- Wesley: for godly people, the worst thing about sin is that it is against God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-39.html

**v. 10**
- Wesley: Those that would be kept from harm, must keep themselves out of harm's way. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-39.html
- Constable: as a slave Joseph was expected to obey her, but as Potiphar's trusted servant he had to refuse, a "no win" position. He also notes that the Hebrew says lie "beside" her. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-39.html
- Pulpit: "to lie by her" is a polite way of speaking, and the words "or to be with her" are not in the original. https://biblehub.com/genesis/39-10.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik and Utley both think she arranged for the house to be empty. Utley adds a rabbinic tradition that it was an Egyptian feast day and she pretended to be sick. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-39/ ; https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- Coffman says Josephus gives the same story. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/genesis-39.html

**v. 12**
- Guzik: God gives a way of escape (1 Cor 10:13), but the believer must take the way out. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-39/
- Wesley: Joseph didn't stop to argue with the temptation. He fled as if running for his life. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-39.html
- Utley defends leaving the garment as the right response to lust (2 Tim 2:22). https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39

**vv. 13–15**
- Utley: she blames her husband and makes a racial slur ("Hebrew"). "Make sport" seems to be an idiom for sexual harassment (cf. 26:8). https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- Clarke links the same word to Isaac and Rebekah in 26:8. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/genesis-39.html
- Coffman: by claiming she cried out, she put herself under a custom later written into law (Deut 22:24) that treated an outcry as proof of innocence. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/genesis-39.html
- Guzik: she avoids saying his name because she didn't want to think of him as a real person. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-39/

**v. 16**
- Gill: she kept the garment as evidence against him. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cev/genesis/39-16.html
- BibleHub study note: Joseph has now been betrayed twice through a garment, first his bloody robe (37:31–33) and now this cloak. https://biblehub.com/genesis/39-16.htm

**vv. 17–18**
- Pulpit: she blames her husband indirectly for bringing the Hebrew into the house. https://biblehub.com/genesis/39-16.htm
- Barnes notes a change in her story. To Potiphar she says the garment was left "by me," not "in her hand," which would have looked suspicious. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cev/genesis/39-16.html

**vv. 19–20**
- Utley: death was the normal penalty for this crime, so Potiphar may have doubted his wife. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- Constable: Joseph's punishment was light. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-39.html
- Guzik quotes a writer (probably Spurgeon) noting that Joseph never accused the woman. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-39/
- Wesley: Potiphar probably chose the worst prison (Ps 105:18). Our Lord Jesus, like Joseph was bound, and numbered with the transgressors. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-39.html

**v. 21**
- Wesley: no gates or bars can shut out God's presence. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-39.html
- Bible.org (Deffinbaugh): God was with Joseph as much in the prison as in the "penthouse." The prison may even have answered his prayers for protection from the woman. https://bible.org/seriespage/39-penthouse-prison-genesis-391-23

**vv. 22–23**
- Utley: the wording echoes v. 6. Joseph was a gifted administrator. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- MacArthur (GTY, Baptist): This isn't natural skill; this is supernatural help. https://www.gty.org/sermons/80-388/joseph-because-god-meant-it-for-good

## 2. Differences between traditions
I found no real disagreement between the traditions, only different emphases:
- **Reformed (Carson, TGC):** God often chooses to bless us in difficult circumstances rather than place us in happier ones. He points to the matching frames of vv. 2–6 and vv. 20–23. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-temptation-of-joseph-genesis-39-en/
- **Methodist (Wesley):** stresses providence preparing Joseph, keeping away from temptation, and Joseph as a picture of Christ. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-39.html
- **Lutheran:** I have Luther only second-hand. Guzik, citing Boice, says Luther saw Joseph as both chaste and prayerful and also as a diligent manager. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-39/

Points where interpreters do differ:
- **Was Potiphar a eunuch?** Guzik leaves it open. Utley says it is probably just a title. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-39/ ; https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-39
- **Who was Potiphar angry at?** Guzik's study guide suggests his anger may have been aimed at his wife, not at Joseph. https://blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/studyguide_gen/gen_39.cfm

## 3. Other views
- **Jewish and later traditions:** Coffman passes on Josephus's version (she promised secrecy and threatened Joseph). Clarke describes the Persian poems in which she is called Zuleekha and finally marries Joseph. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/genesis-39.html ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/genesis-39.html
- **On "success" in vv. 2–3 and 23:** I found no prosperity-teaching sources themselves. Evangelical teachers do warn against a material reading. Deffinbaugh says Joseph's blessings were not to be measured by his bank book, nor will they necessarily be for us. https://bible.org/seriespage/39-penthouse-prison-genesis-391-23 Steven Cole says God's blessing is not necessarily related to favorable circumstances. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-67-true-success-genesis-391-23
